drapeaux.note: Langue d'origine : anglais ; auteur : Ruth Benedict, The Chrysanthemum and the Sword. Retraduite depuis le français, formulation originale à vérifier.
Même phrase de Ruth Benedict (anglais), retraduite depuis le français, avec « écrira-t-elle » inséré au milieu.

titre: Studying a Culture Without Setting Foot in It
accroche: In the middle of the Pacific War, an anthropologist is given the mission of understanding Japan without ever being able to go there.
contenu_vulgarise:
1944. The Pacific War is in full swing, and the American Office of War Information entrusts the anthropologist Ruth Benedict with an unusual mission: to understand Japan, its social organization, its codes of honor, its way of making war, without ever being able to set foot there. The country is at war with the United States; no fieldwork is possible. Benedict has to reconstruct an entire culture from an office in Washington.

## The Fieldwork That Can't Be Done

Out of necessity, she invents a method that will become an object of study in its own right: the “study of a culture at a distance.” She interviews Americans of Japanese descent, some of whom had known the internment imposed after Pearl Harbor, among them her most-cited informant, Robert Hashima, born in the United States but raised in Japan, who returned just before the attack, was interned, and was then recruited by the agency Benedict works for. She watches Japanese films, both propaganda and everyday life, reads translated literature, and combs through the press. “I could not go to Japan,” she would later write, “live in their homes and observe with my own eyes the tensions of everyday life, see what really mattered and what did not.”

## A Book Published After the Fact

The result, *The Chrysanthemum and the Sword*, appeared in 1946, a year after Japan's surrender. It is often repeated that this book convinced General MacArthur to keep Emperor Hirohito on the throne during the occupation; the claim is shakier than it appears, and it is not even known whether MacArthur read it. Another version holds that Benedict herself, as early as 1944, recommended to President Roosevelt that the emperor's reign be maintained under the terms of the coming surrender. But this claim, too, rests on no identified primary or academic source: it circulates without a reference of its own, even on the online encyclopedias that repeat it. What is established, however, is the post Benedict held from 1943 to 1946 at the Office of War Information, where she produced cultural studies of several countries at war (Romania, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Thailand, Japan) before the work on Japan became, once published, her most widely read book.

What the method itself left behind is clear: proof that one can build serious knowledge of a culture without ever having set foot there, provided one multiplies indirect sources and cross-checks them rigorously. The lesson has since been taken up to study societies that are closed or inaccessible to fieldwork.

carte.punch: She described a country without ever setting foot in it.
carte.idee: In 1944, in the middle of the war, Ruth Benedict is given the mission of studying Japan without being able to go there. She invents a method based on interviews, film, and the press, the “study at a distance,” published in 1946 as The Chrysanthemum and the Sword.

quiz.question: Why must the claim that The Chrysanthemum and the Sword convinced MacArthur to keep the emperor be qualified?
choix: Because Benedict never worked for the American government during the war
Because MacArthur publicly denied having read the book
Because the book appeared only after the American occupation of Japan had ended
It is not even known whether MacArthur read the book before setting his occupation policy
quiz.explication: No source establishes that MacArthur read The Chrysanthemum and the Sword, published in 1946 during an occupation that lasted until 1952. The book therefore did come out before the occupation's end. Benedict, for her part, really did work for the Office of War Information from 1943 to 1946, where she produced cultural studies of several countries at war, including Japan.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What materials does Ruth Benedict rely on, being unable to go to Japan?
choix: Interviews, Japanese films, translated literature, and the press
Interrogations of Japanese prisoners of war carried out in the Pacific
Reports from American diplomats who had remained at their posts in Tokyo
Repeated stays in Korea and China, as close as possible to the forbidden field
quiz_supplementaire.explication: She interviews Americans of Japanese descent, watches propaganda films as well as films of everyday life, reads translated literature, and combs through the press. This is what she will call the study of a culture at a distance.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who is Robert Hashima, Benedict's most-cited informant?
choix: A Japanese diplomat stationed in Washington at the time of Pearl Harbor
A translator recruited by the American army during the occupation of Japan
An American born in the United States, raised in Japan, who returned and was then interned
An exiled Japanese anthropologist who had fled his country before the war
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Born in the United States but raised in Japan, Hashima returns just before the attack on Pearl Harbor, undergoes the internment imposed afterward, and is then recruited by the agency Benedict works for.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is known for certain about Benedict's work for the Office of War Information?
choix: That she directed the entire cultural studies program there since 1941
That she worked there only on Japan, at Roosevelt's direct request
That she joined it after the publication of The Chrysanthemum and the Sword, in 1946
That she produced studies there on several countries at war, from 1943 to 1946
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The post held from 1943 to 1946 is the established fact of this episode. There she studies Romania, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Thailand, and Japan, the last of these works becoming, once published, her most widely read book.
